name: Avoiding soy ("soy boy" meta)

card.summary: Skipping soy to protect testosterone; meta-analyses report no hormonal effect in healthy men.
card.note: Term also functions as a political insult.

quick.overview:
Some men avoid soy out of fear its phytoestrogens lower testosterone or feminize them. The "soy boy" insult grew from this idea.

Reported meta-analyses found no effect of soy or isoflavones on male reproductive hormones in healthy people, though the topic is described as still under study.
quick.mechanism: Soy isoflavones resemble estradiol and act on estrogen receptors, the basis of the concern [1].
quick.risks: Reference texts report no hormonal harm from soy in healthy men; soy infant formula has narrow pediatric indications per the American Academy of Pediatrics [2].

lead: Avoiding soy is a dietary practice in which men limit soy foods because they believe soy phytoestrogens lower testosterone or feminize the body, which they associate with less defined, less masculine features. People following it hope to protect muscle-building hormones and a leaner, harder-looking physique and face. The idea is tied to the online insult "soy boy", used for men seen as lacking masculine traits [1].

Soy contains isoflavone phytoestrogens that resemble estradiol and act on estrogen receptors, which prompted early concern [1]. Wikipedia reports that a 2021 meta-analysis found neither soy nor isoflavone intake affects male reproductive hormones in healthy individuals, and a 2021 review concluded soyfoods and isoflavones do not warrant classification as endocrine disruptors [1][2].
The same sources note the topic is still described as under study, with some mixed findings on sperm measures and early concerns raised in 2017 about phytoestrogens as endocrine disruptors [1][2].

angle.text: Followers say cutting soy keeps testosterone and estrogen balance favourable for muscle, body fat and facial structure. Published meta-analyses report no effect of soy or isoflavones on male reproductive hormones in healthy people.

paras: "Soy boy" is a derogatory online term, often aimed at left-leaning men, based on the claim that soy phytoestrogens feminize men [1]. Its modern origin is unclear; it has been attributed to 4chan's /pol/ board and political commentators, and the hashtags #SoyBoy and #MilkTwitter went viral in February 2017 [1]. Earlier, a 1970s article claiming soy disrupts hormone balance is credited with starting soy's negative reputation, though Wikipedia flags that source as possibly unreliable [1].

Proponents claim excess soy causes lowered testosterone and a so-called "soy face", a softer facial look [1]. Wikipedia notes that some conspiracy-oriented commentators have made these claims [1]. In fitness and looksmaxxing circles the practice is framed as avoiding hormone disruption.

Soy phytoestrogens resemble estradiol and act on estrogen receptors, which prompted early concern [1]. Later reviews were more reassuring: a 2010 review found no effect of phytoestrogens on sperm quality or reproductive hormones, a 2018 review found no link between diet-related phytoestrogens and male fertility, and 2021 analyses found no effect of soy or isoflavones on male reproductive hormones in healthy individuals [1]. Some isoflavone studies reported positive effects on sperm measures, and higher soy intake is associated with lower prostate cancer risk [1].

Wikipedia also states that as of 2020 there was insufficient clinical evidence to establish effects of phytoestrogens in humans, and notes that the Linus Pauling Institute describes soy infant formula as a safe alternative where needed [2]. A 2025 meta-analysis found plant-based diets do not compromise muscular strength [1].
Meta-analyses summarised in reference texts, including a 2021 analysis by Reed and colleagues, found no effect of soy or isoflavone intake on reproductive hormones in healthy men [1][2].

timeline.event: Reviews find no effect of phytoestrogens on sperm quality or reproductive hormones [1].
Hashtags #SoyBoy and #MilkTwitter go viral; Rietjens and colleagues raise early endocrine-disruptor concerns [1].
A meta-analysis and a review conclude soy does not affect male reproductive hormones or warrant endocrine-disruptor classification [1].
